title: The Warranty and Indemnity Clause That Keeps the Sale Open Long After Settlement Day
linkedin:
Settlement day is not always the finish line it looks like.

Most Australian SME sale contracts include warranty and indemnity clauses, promises the seller makes about the state of the business that stay live for twelve to twenty-four months after the cheque clears. If any of them turn out to be wrong, the buyer can claim compensation directly from the seller, long after the deal is supposedly done.

This is different to an earnout. An earnout ties part of the price to future performance the buyer controls. A warranty claim is about accuracy at the point of sale, and it can land even if the business goes on to perform exactly as promised.

The claims we typically see are rarely dramatic. Understated leave provisions. A supplier dispute that seemed minor and went undisclosed. Stock valued more generously than an independent check later supports. None of it usually reflects anything the owner did wrong, it reflects how much detail sits inside a business that gets missed when a sale process moves quickly.

The businesses that come through a warranty period cleanly are the ones that did the preparation work months before a buyer was ever at the table, capping total liability, setting a claim threshold, and keeping the warranty period no longer than commercially normal.

Quick one for anyone with a sale somewhere on the horizon, even a distant one. Most business sale contracts include warranty clauses that let a buyer come back and claim money from you for up to two years after settlement, if something you represented about the business turns out to be wrong.

It is usually nothing deliberate. Understated leave provisions, a dispute that seemed minor at the time, stock valued a bit generously. Small stuff that gets missed when a sale process is moving fast.

If you sold tomorrow, how confident are you that your books would hold up to that kind of scrutiny a year from now?

If selling the business is something you are thinking about, even years out, there is one part of the sale contract worth understanding early: the warranty and indemnity clause.

Most business sale agreements include promises the seller makes about the state of the business, accurate accounts, correctly provisioned staff entitlements, no undisclosed disputes. If any of those turn out to be wrong, the buyer can claim compensation from the seller for up to two years after settlement. It is standard practice, not a sign of a bad deal, but it catches owners off guard because it gets far less attention than the headline sale price during negotiations.

The businesses that come through this cleanly are almost always the ones that reviewed their entitlement provisioning, contracts and disclosures well before a buyer was ever at the table, rather than scrambling to answer questions once due diligence started.

For East Coast business owners with a sale anywhere on the horizon, this is worth understanding early. Read the full piece on the blog.
